title: Shorter sliding windows again: short_window = seq//8 (512 -> 256)
description: One line in GPT._compute_window_sizes: short_window = long_window // 4 -> // 8 (512 -> 256), everything else at baseline.
reflection: val_bpb 0.990541 vs my r02 //4 control pair (0.989668 / 0.989981, mean 0.989825): +0.0007, a net LOSS of ~1.2 sd. The window axis is closed at 512; nobody should probe 128. Two corrections that matter more than the number. (1) My FLOP arithmetic in the proposal was wrong: 6 short + 2 long at window 256 is 210.8M FLOPs/token (logged 2.1077e8), a -4.3% cut, not the -8.7% I claimed (I had mistakenly used the all-short attention figure). (2) The throughput tax is now bigger than the arithmetic saving: MFU fell 35.9% -> 33.5% and tokens fell 486.4M -> 474.7M. Going 1024->512 cost ~2 MFU points and still netted +2.5% tokens; going 512->256 cost another ~2.4 points and netted -2.4% tokens. FA3 efficiency per FLOP degrades faster than the window shrinks below 512. Quality-wise the change was not harmful: token-corrected with the -0.000128/1M slope, 474.7M predicts 0.991323 for the //4 config, and I measured 0.990541, a -0.0008 residual in favour of window 256. So the cross-document-contamination story still holds directionally; it is simply no longer purchasable through this knob, because the kernel eats the gain. Implication for a0/a1's long-layer runs: cutting a 2048 layer to 512 removes FLOPs at a window FA3 is already efficient at, so they should convert to tokens better than my run did.
